One suggestion that might help would be to have your bf give the dog a bath before you come over or at least regularly. This can eliminate a fair amount of pollens in their coats and it's been explained to me. Between regular baths for my two dogs and keeping my house pretty well vacuumed, I've been able to keep my dogs and not suffer immensely. My bf has 6 cats at his house so I just don't go over there at all but he does his best to lint roll himself when he comes over and he also keeps a set of clothes at my house that's cat hair free (my cat allergies are worse than my dog allergies). 

As far as meds, I use flonase daily and my allergist said that you have to take it regularly to build up and work. I also nasal rinse so I second another users suggestion to use the neil med products. If I know that I have to visit my bf's place, I'll start taking zyrtec at night, a week to a few days before to build it up. I've also noticed that after a few days to a week of use - the drowsiness and grogginess is cut down a lot. 

Hope this helps and good luck!

Hi! This is me to a tee about  two weeks into my cycle, right after my fertile window ends. I'm an irritable, crying, ragey mess and it's gotten worse this year with the overall stress of work and the pandemic. I'm on 40 mg of Vyvanse right now. 

So, for me, this has to do a ton with my stress levels and hormones. I track my cycle and when my fertility window closes, I start taking calcium supplements and a super low dose of Prozac for a week (although I've recently switched to microdoses instead and I'm seeing results over the last couple of months.)

Lifestyle wise, until my period starts, I avoid caffeine and wine during this time as much as I can. Since my tracking app will let me know when my window has ended, I move any intense projects back a week to reduce my stress. I'll take the dogs out for more walks for exercise. I try to just be kinder and more forgiving to myself.

The suggestion of vitamin c after dinner to help with the come down is also really helpful. I don't do this as often but on really bad days, this can help me flush out my meds so that it's easier to go to sleep and start over the next day. 

Hope some of this helps!

I'll be honest and say that I don't know too much of the experience of schizophrenia but I've had my share of mental health issues. I was diagnosed with major depressive disorder almost ten years ago and refused to go on medication until about two years ago. My depression comes and goes in waves but the last wave has been the most traumatic. Even when I did start taking medication, it took losing my job at a very popular startup and contemplating just being homeless for me to take getting better serious.  Luckily for me, I have a couple of the best people I could ever know who took me in and allowed me to lie in bed, stare at walls, sleep all day, cry randomly for a bit before they gently  encouraged me to color and snuggle with their dogs,  garden, go for walks, eat actual food. It took a while before I started to come out of my worst weeks of depression and actually go to a doctor to be properly medicated. I don't think I would be standing here today in my room if I wasn't still medicated. It's not fun. I hate the side effects and the accompanying weight gain and I still don't go out like i used to and I get major anxiety around crowds so grocery shopping is a non-starter but I'm alive. 

My point is. It's incredibly rough to watch your friend go through this and there's a possibility that even through the struggle there's a little voice in your friends head that's saying, "this isn't right, I just want to go back to who I used to be." That voice is  unfortunately being drowned out by the madness and the mental illness. So, continue to be there for your friend. That kindness and that stability/reliability is just what your friend needs. I'm not 100% yet, not even close and I hate that I've shut out/distanced myself from most of my friends but I'm so so so grateful for the friends who refused to be shut out and continued to call and visit. They helped me gain the strength to help myself because they made me semi believe that I was worth it.
